The roofline: a chase, an evening, one light

A household’s roofline, set every holiday to colors that move, collides with two earlier rulings and raises one new question: whether a chase belongs to the occasion, whether a roof may light itself at dusk, and how several controllers become one light that knows which way round it goes. Today, then three directions for each, none yet picked. Every screen is 1440×900, the size of the wall.

WHY THIS EXISTS

From a household, 30 September and 1 October 2026: an addressable strip along their roofline, set every Christmas, Halloween, Easter and July 4th to colors and effects -- "red and green chasing each other on Christmas", something else for Halloween, something else again for July 4th -- on a Bluetooth SP107E they are replacing with ours. They asked for it done the right way, with no shortcuts. Halloween 2026 is a wish, not a deadline.

Two earlier rulings collide with that, and the hardware adds a third question. design/occasion/ said there are three ambient motions and no fourth, and struck out Theater chase with the zoo; it also said an occasion turns nothing on that was not already on. A roofline is a chase, and a roofline comes on at dusk. And the controller chosen in the hardware repository (strip/README.md, direction C, one per run) makes a roof several boxes that the wall has to show as one light.

Each question is its own page: Today, then three directions, each a whole answer, each with its case on the board and beside it. Every board can be flipped -- the dashed chips at its top right change the occasion, the motion, the moment or the step, and the roof redraws. None is picked yet. When one is, the others move to a Not chosen page with their cases intact.

WHY A COLLECTION OF ITS OWN, AND NOT MORE PAGES IN design/occasion/

design/occasion/ lives apart from design/strip/ on purpose: an occasion is a house feature that a strip happens to render best. Two of these three questions are about occasions, but all three are asked by one object -- a light outside the house, made of several boxes -- and the third is not about occasions at all. Adopting three controllers as one light would be the same question in a year with no holidays in it.

So the questions that amend occasion's rulings are drawn here, against the roof that raised them, and design/occasion/ carries one note pointing here. Whatever is picked updates that collection's rulings in place; its boards stay as the record of the rule before the roof.

Every board draws the same house, so the directions can be laid side by side: a gable over the door and a long eave to the garage, three boxes, four runs -- two of them running against the way you would walk round, because a run always leaves its box, which is true of nearly every real roof.

TODAY -- A STRIP HAS COLORS, AND NOTHING ON IT MOVES

Drawn from the shipped light pane for a strip (the mock house's Under-cabinet strip, opened with a hold, at 1440x900), renamed for the roof: brightness, Automatic, the colors, the three it is used at, and the strip's own row at the foot. Nothing on it moves. The Movement row -- Still, Drifting, Candlelight -- is drawn in design/occasion/Drift.dc.html and unbuilt.

The two facts in the pane's empty foot are the collision. The household's Christmas is a chase, and Drift's list of what not to build struck out Theater chase by name. The question this page answers is whether that line was drawn in the right place, and if a chase comes in, through which door.

A -- THE OCCASION OWNS ITS MOTION

The occasion argument carried one step further. design/occasion/ made Christmas a chip that brings its colors to every light that can show them; A lets it bring its motion too, to the one light that can show motion -- the roofline -- and nowhere else. Four occasions, each drawn once by us: Christmas chases, Halloween is unsteady like embers, Easter drifts, July 4th twinkles. Flip them on the board; the scene card is the shipped Tonight card with the occasion in it.

The zoo stays out because there is nowhere for it to stand: no list of motions is ever shown, only holidays. The household's one control is Hold it still, for a house that wants the colors without the movement. Strips inside take the colors and hold them still -- a chase is for the street, not the sofa.

The cost is that the look is ours. A household whose Christmas has always been red and white has no way to say so here, which is exactly the gap C fills.

B -- A FOURTH WAY FOR A LIGHT TO BE

Reopens "three, and there is no fourth" on its own test: each motion is a way for the household's colors to be, and none takes the color away. A chase passes -- it is their colors, traveling -- and Theater chase was struck out for the company it kept in a list of eighty, not for what it does. So Chasing joins the Movement row on the light's pane, and the occasion brings only its colors.

Flip occasion and movement independently: every combination is one the household could set. That is the strength -- a team's colors chasing on game day, no holiday needed -- and the weakness: Halloween with Candlelight is the household's job to set each October and unset each November, on the light.

Drawn because it is the smallest change; not recommended, because it puts a holiday's motion in a light's settings, which is the walk to every light that the occasion chip was invented to save, and it puts Chasing on every strip indoors too.

C -- A LOOK IS SAID, NOT CHOSEN

The household's own words are the interface. "Christmas: red and green, chasing" is read by a fixed grammar -- colors, one of five words of motion, slowly or quickly -- with no model, the way simple commands already stay deterministic. The house drafts it, plays it on the roof while the draft is open, and keeps it only when told; walking away puts the roof back as it was.

The five words are the three ambient motions under plainer names, plus chasing and twinkling. Asked for "meteor" or "rainbow", the house answers with the five it has rather than guessing, so the vocabulary cannot grow from the screen -- the zoo's door shut a different way. Flip the colors and the word on the board.

On its own it is the least discoverable of the three: a household that never thinks to type gets nothing. It is drawn as a whole answer and recommended as half of one.

WHERE A CHASE RUNS -- THE SAME IN ALL THREE

On the boxes, not streamed from the hub. design/occasion/ said firmware holds the three ambient motions and the brain streams everything else. design/signal/ found the case that argument did not meet -- a fast motion people watch with intent, where a Wi-Fi hiccup reads as a broken light -- and put the drawing on the strip. A chase is that case again, and across several boxes it is harder: each box must know the time and its place along the roof.

So the hub sends each box one description -- colors, motion, speed, a start time, and where its runs sit in the whole -- and each box draws its own frames from a clock the hub keeps them all on (the One light page). A frame is written only when it differs, as the WS2812 rule asks. The roof is given emitter colors, saturated, never the panel's pastels: the boards draw what the LED is asked for.

RECOMMENDED -- A, WITH C AS THE WAY TO CHANGE ONE

A, because the household's own sentence names a holiday before it names a motion, and because it keeps the reasons behind both earlier rulings: on an ordinary night the roof has Still, Drifting and Candlelight and nothing else, and "chase" never becomes a choice anybody scrolls past.

Its one weakness is that the look is ours, and C answers exactly that and nothing more: on an occasion's own pane, "Make it ours" opens the sentence -- their colors, one of the five words -- drafted, played on the roof, kept. The household that does red and white gets red and white, and still never sees a list.

B is the one not to pick. It reopens "no fourth" for every light in the house to solve something that happens in December, outside.

Open: whether strips inside should hold still at Christmas, or chase too when they are long enough to read as a line.

THE QUESTION ON THIS PAGE

"An occasion turns nothing on that was not already on" was written so that a house never lights itself at midnight because it is December. A roofline for Halloween wants to come on at dusk and go off later, every evening of the season, with nobody at the wall.

Every board on this page can be flipped to the same four moments -- Halloween's first dusk, the same night at 11:20 PM, an ordinary July evening, and 3 AM in December -- so the directions answer the same four questions. The last one is the test.

TODAY -- TWO WAYS A ROOF COULD COME ON, AND NEITHER KNOWS THE SEASON

The Tonight card is the shipped one with design/occasion's chip drawn into it; the routine is the shipped Routines page's shape and words (why.ts writes "At sunset"). Flip the moment, and the routine on and off. The occasion alone leaves the roof dark every Halloween evening. The routine alone lights it every evening of the year, in whatever colors it was last left in -- orange in July -- and nothing turns it off, so at 3 AM in December it is on.

The finding is that the rule's reason and its wording have come apart. The reason is surprise: a light on when nobody expected it, inside, at an hour nobody chose. A roofline at dusk in October is not a surprise; it is the point. At 3 AM in December it is.

A -- THE OCCASION HAS A SEASON, AND AN EVENING

Halloween becomes a stretch of evenings: Oct 24 to Nov 1, every year, the roofline on at dusk and off at 11:00. The rule changes from "an occasion turns nothing on" to "an occasion may turn on only the outside lights it was given, only inside its own hours", and the band says so two days before and again as it happens, so the first evening is never a surprise.

Flip the moments: on Halloween's first dusk the roof is lit; at 11:20 PM it is off; on a July evening nothing comes on; at 3 AM in December the house is dark.

What it costs is the shape of the rule. An exception lives inside every occasion, and the roof's hours belong to Halloween instead of to the roof -- a household that wants it lit every evening has to invent an occasion called Evenings.

B -- THE ROOFLINE HAS EVENINGS OF ITS OWN

Separates the two questions A ties together. WHEN is the light's: an outside light is asked once, at the end of its setup, whether it keeps evenings -- "Most rooflines are on from dusk until bedtime. Shall this one?" -- and the answer lives on its pane, like a porch light's. WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE is the season's: whatever occasion is on colors it, and on an ordinary evening it is warm white.

The rule stays exactly as written. An occasion turns nothing on; the roof turns on because it was asked to keep evenings, by the household, in words, once. Flip the moments and the three settings: "Only in an occasion" is A's answer as a setting, for a roof nobody wants lit in March.

The cost is two places to look when the roof does something, and the answer to "why is it on?" has to name the right one.

C -- THE HOUSE ASKS, AT DUSK

The strictest reading: nothing ever comes on by itself. At dusk inside an occasion the band offers the roofline once -- "It's dusk, and it's Halloween. Light the roofline until 11:00?" -- on the wall and every phone at home. Tap Light it on the board to see the roof lit; flip the moment to see that nothing is asked in July or at night.

It keeps the rule without a single exception, and it is the cheapest to build. But it hands the household back the chore they asked to be rid of, nine evenings in a row, and the one evening they are out is the one the street sees dark.

Drawn as the record of the strictest answer, and kept as the rung below B for a household that says no to evenings.

WHAT ALL THREE KEEP

Nothing inside the house ever comes on for an occasion. Dusk is the house's own -- it already knows sunset for routines, and dusk is a little after it, so the roof does not light in daylight. Every time the roof comes on by itself the band says so, and the line is the undo, as every arrival's line is. An evening ends at a time the household can see and change, 11:00 unless told otherwise, never "until sunrise".

And whichever is picked, the wall can always answer "why is it on?" in one sentence, which is the sentence each board prints under its timeline.

RECOMMENDED -- B, WITH A'S SEASONS FOR WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE

B, because it keeps the rule whole and its reason true: an occasion still turns nothing on, and the roof keeps evenings because the roof was asked to, once, on its own pane, the way a porch light is. When is the light's, all year; how it looks is the season's.

A's dates are then how a season starts and ends itself -- Halloween's colors from Oct 24 to Nov 1 with nobody touching the chip -- which is A's best part without A's exception.

C is kept as the strictest answer and as the rung below: a household that says no to evenings at setup can still be offered the roof at dusk, in the band.

Open: whether "Only in an occasion" should be the default for a roofline, since most households do not light the eaves in March.

THE QUESTION ON THIS PAGE

The roof is two or three controllers, each with up to two runs, each installed where its runs start. The wall has to show them as one light; a chase has to travel from one to the next in order; and the household has to tell the house that order -- which run comes after which, and which way each one runs -- without ever meeting the words output, data, segment or offset.

The second board is what all three directions share. The three after it differ on one thing only: how the house learns the way round.

TODAY -- THREE BOXES, THREE LIGHTS

What the house would do now with three controllers: adopt each as its own strip -- Light strip, Light strip 2, Light strip 3 -- each with its own pane, its own Off and its own name, and (docs/strip.md, item 51) a second run that shows what the first does until told otherwise.

Flip "Asked for a chase": each box chasing from its own first light, on its own clock. Two runs crash at the peak, two over the garage, and none of the three is in step. The roof the household thinks of as one thing is three things to the house, and nothing in the house knows the order of the runs or which way one goes.

WHAT ALL THREE SHARE -- ONE ROOFLINE ON THE WALL

Whatever answers the order, the wall shows one Roofline: one tile, one pane, one Off, the occasion's look across all of it. The boxes appear only on the pane, named by where they are, and only to say something -- Fine, or why one part is dark, in the words its guard already reports (item 51: a supply of the wrong kind, a switch that tripped, a miswired line). Flip "Garage end dark": the tile stays one light, and the dark part says what to check.

A second box joins at the last beat of its own setup, which is otherwise unchanged: "Is this more of the Roofline, or a light of its own?" The hub keeps every box on one clock and tells each where its runs sit along the roof and which way each goes. That last fact is the only thing the three directions disagree about.

A -- TAP THEM IN THE ORDER THEY GO ROUND

The roof is put on show: every run lit in its own color, with a white light running along it the way it goes. Standing in the yard with a phone, the household taps the colors in the order they would walk past them; a run whose white light comes back toward where they started is tapped twice to turn it round. Then one white light goes round the whole roof, the way they said, and they say whether it goes the right way.

Flip Before, Halfway and Done. Nothing is named but colors -- no word about data, ends, outputs or boxes. It is the same screen for two boxes or six, for a roof that went up in any order, and the same screen the day a fourth box is added.

It needs the roof in view, which a roof that wraps the house is not from any one spot.

B -- THE ORDER COMES FROM PUTTING THEM UP

Each box is set up on the ground (the press, as for any strip), clicked onto its rail, and when it powers up the house asks two things: more of the Roofline? and -- by running one white light round from the start and into the new box -- did it carry on? The guess is that a box continues from the one added before it, which is right whenever a person puts the roof up in order. Flip the guess to the wrong one: the light jumps to the far end and runs back.

It learns the order in the moment it is made and asks nothing at the end. But it asks on a ladder, and it does nothing for a roof that is already up -- every box of a household moving from an SP107E is already up, so for them it is A, asked three times.

C -- THE ORDER IS NEVER ASKED

Every run moves away from its own box, which the house knows as a fact, not a guess: a run's first light is always at its board. Nobody is asked anything, and setup is the indoor strip's, box after box.

Flip the occasions to see the finding: only a chase shows it. Flickering, twinkling, still and drifting look the same with or without an order, because they have no direction. A chase shows the seams -- two runs meeting head on at the peak and over the garage, two bursts leaving the middle box both ways -- marked on the roof.

So C is the right answer until a chase is wanted, and the wrong one after. That is why it is part of the recommendation: it is what the roof does before the question is asked.

RECOMMENDED -- A, STARTED FROM B'S GUESS, WITH C UNTIL IT IS ANSWERED

C is what the roof does before anybody says anything: every run away from its box, never wrong, only not continuous -- and for every motion but a chase it is indistinguishable from the order being known. So the question is only needed for a chase, and it can wait until a chase is first wanted: "Christmas goes round the house. Show it which way round?"

When it is asked, A: the household looks at their own roof and taps colors, with the order filled in from B's guess (the order the boxes were added), so the common case is one look and one tap.

B alone is not picked: it asks at the top of a ladder and fails every roof already up -- which is this household's.

Open: a roof that wraps the house, where no one spot sees every run. A handles it in two passes; whether the phone should lead the household round the corner is a board of its own.

THE QUESTION ON THIS PAGE

The One light page drew the Roofline's own pane with its boxes on it, by place, and the way round, its evenings and Hold it still beside them (OneLight). The build, merged 1 October 2026 as PR #44, put the roofline into every light's pane instead -- brightness, Automatic, the colors, Reading, Evening and Night -- with one row at its foot that opens a sheet holding the rest. The builder's reason was fit: the board's parts and a lamp's pane together would not go on the wall without scrolling.

That is true, and it makes this a question about what to take away rather than what to hide. Today is the build, drawn from the running mock; then three whole panes at 1440x900, each with the mock house's roof -- three boxes, four runs, two of them turned round, Christmas showing. Every board flips the garage end dark (the dashed chips at its top right), so each answers the same question: is the garage end working, and what do I do about it?

TODAY -- EVERY LIGHT'S PANE, AND ONE ROW INTO A SHEET

Drawn from app/src/panes/LightPane.vue and StripSheet.vue running against the mock at ?roofline=christmas, held open from the Backyard on a 1440x900 wall, in the values the panel computes there; flip to the sheet the row opens. Everything on the pane but its last row is what a table lamp has: Automatic, eight colors and More colors, and the three it is used at. The roofline is that last row -- "Three boxes, four runs · 412 lights", with the look under it.

The sheet holds what OneLight put on the pane: the boxes by place, Which way round, Its evenings, and Moving or Hold it still. Flip Garage end dark: the room's tile already says so ("On · the garage end is dark"), the row's second line becomes "Garage end: dark" in gray, and what to do about it -- plug the 12 V supply back in -- is in the sheet, in red.

The measure of it: of the 500 by 548 beside the brightness column, the roof's own facts get 112 at the foot; the rest goes to colors the season overrides and three levels nobody reads a roof by.

A -- AS BUILT: ONE ROW INTO A SHEET

The build, kept as it is, with the walk drawn on it. To answer "is the garage end working?" a household holds the Roofline's tile in the Backyard (1), taps the row at the foot of the pane (2), and reads the third line of the sheet (3). Flip the board between the pane and the sheet, and the garage end between Fine and Dark.

For it: the pane is every light's pane, so nothing about a light is learned twice, and on a night with nothing wrong the roof's own facts are one row nobody needs to open. The tile already says when part of the roof is dark, so the alarm is never a tap away -- only the reason is.

Against it: what the roof needs is one tap deeper than what it does not. Hold it still, which the Movement page made the household's one control over a look, is in the sheet; the eight colors, which the season overrides, are on the pane. And the row says "Garage end: dark" in the same gray it says "Christmas" in, so the pane is the one place where a fault does not look like one.

B -- THE ROOF'S OWN PANE: WHAT IS GENERIC GIVES WAY

Asks of each part of a light's pane whether a roofline needs it. Brightness, yes: it stays the same column in the same place it has on every light. Automatic, the colors and More colors, no: the season decides a roof's colors, and a look of the household's own is said in the command box (the Movement page, A with C), so "Say another look" is its door. Reading, Evening and Night, no: nobody reads by a roof.

What that frees is exactly enough. The right column holds What it is showing -- the look, drawn small in the roof's own emitter colors, with Moving or Hold it still -- When it comes on, and Which way round. The left column, which on every light carries the light's facts, carries the boxes by place, left to right as they go round, each saying Fine or Dark with its runs drawn lit; and the pane's sentence, which on a lamp says "On at 35%, by hand", says why the roof is on, or what is wrong and what to do. Nothing scrolls.

Flip Garage end dark: the sentence leads in red with what to do, and the third box goes dark where it sits. The cost: past its first column a roofline's pane no longer looks like a lamp's, and a household that wants one fixed color on the roof has to say it rather than tap it.

C -- THE ROOF, DRAWN

The pane's floor becomes the roofline itself, as the house knows it: the lights in the order they go round, each run as long as it is, an arrow over each for the way it leaves its box, and the three boxes under it by place. It is not a picture of the gable -- nobody has told the house the shape of the roof, only the order, the lengths and which way each run goes -- but it is the same description each box is sent, drawn, so it cannot disagree with the roof.

So "is the garage end working?" is answered from across the room: flip Garage end dark and that stretch is dark where it is, ringed, with what to do under it. The way round is on the drawing instead of behind a row, and Which way round is the door to the yard (TapA). Brightness lies along the top of the controls -- the panel's own bar, the shape a narrow screen already uses -- so the look and the evenings sit side by side under it, and the roof gets the width of the wall.

The costs: brightness changes shape on this one light while every other pane keeps a column; the drawing is new work to build and to pin with a test; and until the way round is known (the One light page: it is not asked until a chase is first wanted) the line can only show each box's runs apart, unjoined, with Which way round as the ask.

RECOMMENDED -- C, WITH B IF BRIGHTNESS MUST STAY A COLUMN

Not A. The build's reason was true -- the board's parts and a lamp's pane do not fit on one wall together -- but the answer is to take away what a roof never uses, not to hide what it does. A keeps eight colors on the pane and Hold it still in a sheet, which is the Movement ruling upside down, and it shows a fault in the gray it shows Christmas in.

C, because the roofline is the one light on the wall whose state has a place, and the pane is where a household should see that place: which part is lit, which way it runs, which part is dark and why, at a glance, with nothing opened. It draws only what the house knows, so it is honest on any roof, and it makes the way round something you can see is right rather than a setting that says "Set".

B if the household would rather every light kept its brightness column where it is. It carries every fact C does, in words, and is the smaller step from the build: the rig keeps its shape and only what is in it changes.

Whichever is picked, the arrangement is pinned with a test the way app/tests/rooms.test.ts pins the Rooms tab, and the others move to a Not chosen page with their cases.

Open: a roof of five or six boxes. C's line holds them, only denser; B's three tiles do not, and would become rows.

THE QUESTION ON THIS PAGE

The pane page decided C: the roof drawn across the floor of the Roofline's pane, under both columns (DrawnC). The board drew a house that does not share its lights with other apps. In one that does, every light's pane carries one more quiet row under its name -- Shared with other apps, Shared or Kept home, and a sentence saying what that means -- and that row makes the left column 127 taller than the board's. The roof, starting where the board starts it, would then run under the percentage.

The build (PR #46) answered it alone: in that case the roof keeps to the right-hand column and the left column runs the full height beside it. That is a composition nobody chose, so it is drawn here before anything is built on it. Today is the build with the house sharing; then three whole panes at 1440x900, each keeping DrawnC's idea intact -- the roof drawn as the house knows it, a dark run dark where it is. Every board flips the garage end dark (the dashed chips at its top right).

A page of its own rather than the pane page, because that page's question is closed and carries its own Today, its own recommendation and the note saying what was decided; this is a second question about the same pane, and it should be read, and decided, apart from the first.

TODAY -- SHARED WITH OTHER APPS, THE ROOF KEEPS TO THE RIGHT

Drawn from the running mock at ?room=backyard&roofline=christmas with SHARED=held, held open on a 1440x900 wall, in the values the panel computes there (app/src/Opened.vue, app/src/RoofPlate.vue, panel.css's .pane-roof:has(.pane-said .opened-kind)). The share row sits under the name, from 363 to 480; the round buttons move from 379 down to 506, the percentage to 602, and the sentence ends at 716.

So the roof moves: the plate is 748 wide under the controls instead of 1,342 under both columns, its line drawn one dot to four lights rather than one to two, 28 to a run where the board drew 55. Everything it says is still there -- the order round, the arrows, the three boxes by place, a dark run ringed with its next step under it, and nothing scrolls. What it costs is the width, and the corner under the left column, which is empty from 716 to the foot of the wall.

The same rule fires for any quiet row in that column, not only this one: Show this as, Lead with, and Take it out of the house while the pane is being edited. The pinned test is app/e2e/controller.spec.ts, "in a house sharing its lights with other apps, the roof keeps to the right and still nothing scrolls".

A -- THE ROOF KEEPS TO THE RIGHT

The build's answer, drawn as a direction and marked with what it costs. The left column is every light's left column, share row and all, at its own height; the roof keeps to the right-hand column under the bar and the two cards. Flip Not shared: that is DrawnC, the same light on the same evening, and the roof is back across the wall.

For it: nothing new is drawn and nothing is folded. The share row looks and works exactly as it does on a lamp's pane, one tap to Kept home, with the sentence that says what sharing means. It is already built and tested, and it holds any quiet row the left column grows, not only this one.

Against it: a setting about other apps decides how wide the roof is drawn. The line that was chosen because it reads from across the room is drawn at 748 instead of 1,342 (1), at half its density, its three places drawn closer together -- and under the left column the wall is empty (2), so the pane is lopsided: full on the right, short on the left. And the roof moves when the house starts or stops sharing, which nobody touching the Roofline did.

B -- SHARING IS SAID BY THE ROOM

The share row folds to one quiet word on the room's line: Backyard, then Shared with other apps in a small chip with the light's own color as its dot, or Kept out of other apps with none. A light's other facts -- where it is, what it is called -- are said on those two lines already, and whether other apps can see it is one more fact of that kind. It takes no height, so the pane is DrawnC to the pixel whether the house shares or not, and the roof keeps the width of the wall.

Flip Opened: tapping the chip opens the same row over the name -- Shared and Kept home, and the sentence saying Apple Home, Google Home and Alexa can see it -- as a small card that closes when the pane is touched anywhere else. After a choice the chip says what the light now is, so it is its own undo, and nothing under the finger goes anywhere.

The costs: changing it is two taps where it was one, and a card opened over the pane is new to the pane -- the nearest thing it has is Show this as, which opens in place. On this light the share row no longer looks like a lamp's; whether every pane should say it this way is a question for those panes, not answered here.

C -- THE BAR MAKES ROOM

Asks what in the right-hand column has width to spare, and the answer is the bar: 748 across for one number. It gives up 236, and sharing takes the end of the row as a pill the bar's height and shape, labeled the way the bar is labeled -- OTHER APPS over Shared and Kept home, still one tap. The left column is DrawnC's, the look and the evenings are DrawnC's, and the roof keeps the width of the wall. Flip Not shared and the bar is whole again; that is the only thing on the pane that moves.

Not the evenings, which was the other place to look: folding them to one line would put Every evening, Only in an occasion and Not by itself behind a tap, and the pane page ruled that what a roof uses stays on the pane, not behind a row.

The costs: a setting changed once a year sits on the row with the control used every evening, at the same weight. The sentence saying what sharing means does not fit in a pill, so OTHER APPS has to carry it alone. And the bar's length now depends on a setting about other apps -- a smaller version of A's fault.

RECOMMENDED -- B

Not A. It is honest, and it fits, but it lets a setting about other apps decide how much of the wall the roof gets, and it makes the pane change shape when nobody touched the Roofline. DrawnC was chosen for the drawing across the wall; A gives it up in exactly the houses that have done the most to set the hub up.

B, because sharing is a fact about the light, set once and then read, and the room's line is where the pane says facts about the light. It keeps the chosen pane exactly as it was chosen, in every house, and still shows at a glance whether Alexa can ask for the roof. The second tap is a fair price for a setting nobody changes in December.

C if the household would rather sharing stayed one tap. It also keeps the roof whole, at the cost of a shorter bar and the sentence that explains sharing.
